sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Narasiṃha** (*narasimha*) — Man-Lion Avatar · The Man-Lion — the fourth avatāra of Viṣṇu — belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Man-Lion Avatar". The name means "The Man-Lion — the fourth avatāra of Viṣṇu"[^1].

**Narasiṃha** belongs to the Sanskrit tradition, where it is associated with man-lion avatar.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Narasiṃha** and serves its temple at [narasimha.com](https://punicodex.com/narasimha/). The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *narasimha* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The name is attested in Devanagari as **नरसिंह**. Etymologically it means "The Man-Lion — the fourth avatāra of Viṣṇu"[^1].

Sanskrit Narasiṃha, from nara 'man' + siṃha 'lion'; the man-lion avatāra of Viṣṇu who slew Hiraṇyakaśipu.

The ASCII form *narasimha* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Narasiṃha** recovers the full diacritic detail of the scholarly transliteration directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves at least one distinctive feature — a diacritic or a distinctive letter — that the ASCII form loses, and exactly one historically valid Unicode restoration exists, which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **n** → **N** — Same, capitalized
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **s** → **s** — Same
- **i** → **i** — Same
- **m** → **ṃ** — M with dot: anusvara
- **h** → **h** — Same
- **a** → **a** — Same

The canonical temple for this name is served at **narasimha.com**[^2].

sources.citation: Monier Monier-Williams, A Sanskrit-English Dictionary, Oxford; Cologne Digital Sanskrit Dictionaries, 1899.

sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/narasimha/** — Sanskrit Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **N** — Initial character of the restored form Narasiṃha.
- **arasiṃha** — Remainder of the name, preserving the distinctive marks of the Sanskrit tradition.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'NARASIMHA' — pronounce the restored form with attention to the preserved diacritics and length.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Sanskrit** — Narasiṃha, the restored Unicode form of the name

Narasiṃha is Tier 1 because the Sanskrit form preserves distinctive features that ASCII loses: stress, length, or special characters.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The stories of **Narasiṃha** circulate within the Sanskrit corpus, where the figure embodies man-lion avatar.[^1]

### Primary Attestation (Sources)

Narasiṃha is attested in the canonical Sanskrit sources as a figure associated with man-lion avatar.[^2]

### Name and Meaning (Etymology)

The name means "The Man-Lion — the fourth avatāra of Viṣṇu" and reflects the figure's role in the tradition. **Narasiṃha** is the man-lion avatāra of Viṣṇu who destroys the demon Hiraṇyakaśipu. Appearing from a pillar at dusk, he uses claws rather than weapons to circumvent the demon's boons of invulnerability.[^1] The myth celebrates divine ingenuity and the protection of the devout child Prahlāda. The image of Narasiṃha bursting from the pillar became a favorite iconographic subject, representing the omnipresence of divine protection in places where violence is forbidden.[^2]

sources.citation: Rāmāyaṇa, Vālmīki; translated by Hari Prasad Shastri, 500 BCE.

sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
Narasiṃha appears within the Sanskrit tradition and has influenced later retellings, artistic depictions, and scholarly study. The Unicode restoration preserves the name's distinctive orthography for contemporary use.[^1]

Within the Sanskrit tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[amsa|Aṃśa]], [[daksa|Dakṣa]], [[dhatr|Dhātṛ]], [[durga|Durgā]], [[ganesha|Gaṇeśa]], and [[ganga|Gaṅgā]].

sections.body: Narasiṃha continues to appear in scholarship, art, and popular reception as a significant figure of the Sanskrit tradition. Restoring the name in Unicode returns the original marks that ASCII removes.[^1] Narasiṃha is a popular subject in South Indian temple sculpture, dance drama, and festival iconography.[^1]

sections.label: Vedic References
sections.body:
The man-lion form of Viṣṇu is prefigured in Vedic hymns that celebrate divine rescue from calamity and the power of a deity to assume any shape.[^1] The **Narasimha Puruṣa** of later Vedic recensions becomes the model for the Bhāgavata narrative in which the Man-Lion tears apart Hiraṇyakaśipu.[^2]

Vedic theophany thus supplies the theological grammar for the avatāra.
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Upaniṣads
sections.body:
The **Narasimha Tāpanīya Upaniṣad** interprets the man-lion avatāra as a symbol of the soul's liberation: the pillar from which Narasimha emerges is the syllable Oṃ, and his claws represent knowledge cutting through ignorance.[^1] The **Chāndogya** and **Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣads** provide the wider Vedāntic context.[^2]

The myth is thereby transformed from martial narrative to soteriology.
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Purāṇas
sections.body:
The **Bhāgavata Purāṇa** (Canto 7) gives the classic account of Narasimha's emergence from a palace pillar to destroy the tyrant Hiraṇyakaśipu and save his devotee Prahlāda.[^1] The **Viṣṇu Purāṇa** and **Nṛsiṃha Purāṇa** expand the liturgical and iconographic details.[^2]

These Purāṇas fix the narrative that dominates Hindu temple worship.
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Mantras & Stotras
sections.body:
The **Narasiṃha Gāyatrī** and **Ugra-Nṛsiṃha Mūla Mantra** are recited for protection and the destruction of enemies, both internal and external.[^1] Tantric and Āgamic traditions prescribe specific mantras for the fierce (*ugra*) and benevolent (*saumya*) forms of the deity.[^2]

The mantras identify Narasimha as a guardian whose roar dispels fear.

sections.body: Narasiṃha embodies man-lion avatar in the Sanskrit imagination. The name's restoration is not merely cosmetic: it recovers the stress, length, and script that make the figure recognizable in the source tradition.[^1]
